ranking.rationale: Age is a strong, broadly causal predictor of food-stamp eligibility and need through lifecycle effects on earnings, household composition, disability, and work capacity, and it is likely to remain predictive across domains better than state, year, race, nativity, or other potentially shortcut-heavy identifiers.

Family worker count is a strong, semantically stable proxy for household economic capacity and SNAP eligibility beyond age alone. It should generalize across states/years better than location or demographic identity features, and is less leakage-prone than public coverage or brittle high-cardinality identifiers like occupation/place of birth.

Household presence/age of children is a strong, semantically stable predictor of SNAP receipt because eligibility and need are tightly linked to supporting children, and it adds household-need information not captured by age or spouse status. It is more robust across domains than state/year identifiers or demographic shortcut variables like race, sex, nativity, and less leakage-prone than public coverage.

Educational attainment is a strong, broadly causal correlate of income and SNAP eligibility that should remain predictive across states and years. It adds substantial stable socioeconomic signal beyond age, family structure, and spouse presence, while being less domain-specific and less leakage-prone than state, year, race, citizenship, or public-coverage variables.

Usual hours worked adds strong, broadly stable signal about labor-market attachment and economic need beyond age, family structure, and education. It is more semantically tied to SNAP eligibility/need than demographic or geography-coded variables, and is less likely than state, race, nativity, or occupation to act as a brittle domain identifier.

Weeks worked is a strong, semantically stable proxy for annual labor-market attachment and income adequacy, which directly relates to food-stamp eligibility and need. It adds substantial signal beyond age, household structure, education, and usual hours worked by capturing persistence of employment over the year. It is less likely than state, year, race, sex, nativity, or occupation to act as a domain identifier or brittle demographic shortcut.

Worked-last-week adds strong, semantically stable signal about current labor-force attachment and income scarcity that is directly relevant to SNAP eligibility/use, while complementing already selected hours and weeks worked. It is less likely than state, year, race, nativity, or place-of-birth variables to encode domain identity or brittle demographic shortcuts, and more broadly reliable than narrower unemployment-status indicators like layoff or looking-for-work.

Disability status adds strong, semantically stable signal for SNAP/Food Stamps eligibility and need beyond age, household composition, education, and work-intensity features already selected. It is less likely than state/year, race, citizenship, birthplace, or occupation to act as a domain identifier or brittle shortcut, and more directly captures persistent barriers to earnings and employment than narrower disability subtypes.

Job search status adds strong, semantically stable signal for SNAP eligibility beyond hours/weeks worked and work status, capturing current labor-market distress without relying on explicit domain identifiers or more brittle demographic shortcuts.

Cognitive difficulty is a strong, semantically stable indicator of economic vulnerability and reduced work capacity that should generalize across domains. It adds meaningful signal beyond age, disability, and employment variables while being less likely than state, year, race, nativity, or citizenship features to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Household relationship adds stable signal about family composition and dependency structure that is directly relevant to SNAP/Food Stamps eligibility and need, while being less domain-specific than state/year and less shortcut-prone than race, citizenship, or birthplace. It complements already selected spouse/household variables by distinguishing child, parent, and other dependent roles not yet captured.

Marital status adds stable household-structure and economic-responsibility signal for SNAP eligibility beyond age, relationship, spouse presence, and work variables. It is broadly causal/semantic across domains, while alternatives like state/year are domain identifiers and race/citizenship/nativity/place-of-birth/English are more likely to act as demographic shortcuts or shift-sensitive proxies.

Public health coverage is a strong, semantically relevant proxy for low income and program eligibility that should remain predictive across domains. It adds complementary signal beyond age, disability, work, education, and family structure, while being less domain-identifying and less likely to encode brittle geographic or demographic shortcuts than state, race, nativity, citizenship, or place-of-birth features.

Hearing difficulty adds stable, semantically relevant signal about disability-related barriers and reduced earning capacity that plausibly increase SNAP eligibility/use, while being less domain-specific than state/year and less shortcut-prone than race, sex, nativity, or citizenship. It complements already selected DIS by refining functional limitation severity without relying on brittle geographic or demographic identifiers.

Vision difficulty adds stable signal about disability-related barriers and economic vulnerability that is directly relevant to SNAP eligibility/need, while being less domain-specific than state/year and less likely to act as a demographic shortcut than race, sex, nativity, citizenship, ancestry, or place of birth. It complements already selected disability indicators without relying on brittle geographic or policy identifiers.

Recent childbirth is a strong, semantically stable indicator of household need and SNAP eligibility pressure, adding family-resource strain information not already captured by age, marital/relationship status, work variables, disability, or education. It is more causally tied to food assistance demand than demographic identity or domain-marker features like state, year, race, nativity, citizenship, or place of birth.

Layoff status adds direct, semantically stable signal about recent employment disruption and income instability, which is highly relevant to food-stamp eligibility/use. It complements already selected work-intensity features without relying on geography, race, citizenship, or other domain-identifying demographics that are more brittle under distribution shift.

Occupation adds substantial stable signal about earnings capacity and employment quality beyond hours/weeks worked, education, and disability, which are central determinants of SNAP eligibility. It is more semantically tied to need than demographic or domain-ID features, and is less likely than state/year/race/sex/nativity-related variables to encode brittle shifts or shortcut correlations across Tableshift domains.

Citizenship status adds stable signal about SNAP eligibility and household economic vulnerability beyond age, education, work, disability, and family structure. It is more semantically tied to benefit access than ancestry, race, sex, or state/year, and is less brittle than place-of-birth proxies while still capturing meaningful variation relevant across domains.

English proficiency adds stable signal about immigrant integration and barriers to employment/program access that can affect SNAP eligibility and take-up, while being less direct as a domain identifier than state/year and less problematic than race/place-of-birth proxies. It complements already selected education, work, citizenship, disability, and family-structure features with meaningful but not overly brittle socioeconomic information.

Military service adds some stable signal about household economic status and eligibility-related life circumstances beyond age, work, disability, and education, while being less likely than state, year, race, sex, nativity, ancestry, or place of birth to act primarily as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Nativity adds broad, semantically stable signal about SNAP eligibility and household economic vulnerability beyond education, language, citizenship, and work variables, while being less brittle and less domain-identifying than state/year and less shortcut-prone than race/ancestry/place-of-birth.

Sex can add stable marginal signal for SNAP/food-stamp eligibility and household economic structure beyond age, marital status, relationship, fertility, work, and disability, while being less domain-specific and less likely to act as direct environment ID than state/year or highly brittle origin/race variables.

Race can add some stable signal for SNAP eligibility through persistent structural disparities not fully captured by age, education, work, disability, family structure, and citizenship. It is less directly a domain identifier than state or survey year, and likely offers more marginal predictive value than ancestry or place of birth given NATIVITY/CIT/ENG are already selected.

Place of birth can add some stable signal about household eligibility and economic integration beyond citizenship, nativity, English ability, and education, while being less directly tied to benchmark domain splits than state or survey year and less redundant/socially brittle than ancestry.

Ancestry may add a small amount of stable household-context signal beyond nativity, birthplace, race, and language, while being less directly tied to benchmark domain splits than state or survey year. State is typically a domain identifier in Tableshift and year can encode temporal/domain artifacts, so both should be penalized for OOD generalization.

Survey year can add limited stable signal by capturing broad policy and macroeconomic shifts affecting SNAP eligibility and take-up across all domains, whereas state is primarily a domain identifier in TableShift and is more likely to induce brittle shortcut learning and hurt out-of-distribution generalization.

State is the only remaining feature, but it should be strongly downweighted: in ACS food stamp prediction it mainly captures geography-specific policy, administration, and cost-of-living differences that often define train/test domain shifts rather than stable household-level need. With ACS_YEAR already selected, ST adds mostly domain identification and brittle regional shortcuts, so its marginal stable predictive value is low.
